system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: FLP impossibility
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The bivalence/univalence argument showing that deterministic asynchronous agreement is impossible with one crash failure. Covers the existence of an initial bivalent configuration, the commutation case analysis for staying bivalent, and the extension to shared memory. Excludes the circumvention techniques (randomization, failure detectors) except as boundary conditions.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C01-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A configuration that is not bivalent is univalent, and it is 0-valent or 1-valent according to whether all executions starting in it produce 0 or 1 as the decision value.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0122-s17] A conﬁguration that is not bivalent is univalent, or more speciﬁcally 0-valent or 1-valent depending on whether all executions starting in the conﬁguration produce 0 or 1 as the decision value.
- CS-DIST-C01-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A configuration $C$ is bivalent if there exist traces $T_0$ and $T_1$ starting from $C$ that lead to configurations $CT_0$ and $CT_1$ in which all processes decide 0 and 1 respectively.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0122-s16] The guidepost for this strategy is the notion of bivalence, where a conﬁguration C is bivalent if there exist traces T0 and T1 starting from C that lead to conﬁgurations CT0 and CT1 where all processes decide 0 and 1 respectively.
- CS-DIST-C01-S1-03.r1 | S1
  ATOM: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result says that agreement cannot be achieved in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0120-s10] The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result [FLP85] says something much stronger: you can’t do agreement in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.1 After its initial publication, it was quickly generalized to other models including asynchronous shared memory [LAA87], and indeed the presentation of the result in [Lyn96, §12.2] is given for shared- memory ﬁrst, with the original result appearing in [Lyn96, §17.2.3] as a corollary of the ability of message passing to simulate shared memory.
- CS-DIST-C01-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: An initial bivalent configuration exists. If all initial configurations were univalent, two that differ only in process $p$'s input would both be $x$-valent, because executions with $p$ faulty are indistinguishable to the other processes. Chaining such configurations would make all initial configurations $x$-valent, which violates validity.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0123-s09] Otherwise, let C and C′ be two initial conﬁgurations that diﬀer only in the input of one process p; by assumption, both C and C′ are univalent.
    [CS-DIST-p0123-s10] Consider two executions starting with C and C′ in which process p is faulty; we can arrange for these executions to be indistinguishable to all the other processes, so both decide the same value x.
    [CS-DIST-p0123-s11] It follows that both C and C′ are x-valent.
    [CS-DIST-p0123-s12] But since any two initial conﬁgurations can be connected by some chain of such indistinguishable conﬁgurations, we have that all initial conﬁgurations are x-valent, which violations validity.
- CS-DIST-C01-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: If $e$ and $e'$ are steps of the same process $p$, the other processes can run a finite sequence of steps with no message from $p$ delivered until some process decides. That execution is indistinguishable to all processes except $p$ from the one starting with $De'e$, so the same value is decided in both, contradicting $Dee'$ being 0-valent and $De'e$ being 1-valent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s11] Now suppose e and e′ are steps of the same process p.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s14] But now we consider some ﬁnite sequence of steps e1e2 . . . ek in which no message sent by p is delivered and some process decides in Dee1 . . . ek (this occurs since the other processes can’t distinguish Dee′ from the conﬁguration in which p died in D, and so have to decide without waiting for messages from p).
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s15] This execution fragment is indistinguishable to all processes except p from De′ee1 . . . ek, so the deciding process decides the same value i in both executions.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s16] But Dee′ is 0-valent and De′e is 1-valent, giving a contradiction.
- CS-DIST-C01-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: In the case analysis, suppose $De$ is 0-valent and $De'e$ is 1-valent, with $e$ and $e'$ steps of different processes. Then $Dee' = De'e$, because in an asynchronous system one cannot tell which process received its message first. Since $De$ is 0-valent, $Dee'$ is also 0-valent, which contradicts $De'e$ being 1-valent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s06] Suppose e and e′ are steps of diﬀerent processes p and p′.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s07] Let both steps go through in either order.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s08] Then Dee′ = De′e, since in an asynchronous system we can’t tell which process received its message ﬁrst.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s09] But De is 0-valent, which implies Dee′ is also 0-valent, which contradicts De′e being 1-valent.
- CS-DIST-C01-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: When steps $e$ and $e'$ belong to different processes, they commute, so $Dee' = De'e$. Then $De$ being 0-valent forces $Dee'$ to be 0-valent, which contradicts $De'e$ being 1-valent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s06] Suppose e and e′ are steps of diﬀerent processes p and p′.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s07] Let both steps go through in either order.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s08] Then Dee′ = De′e, since in an asynchronous system we can’t tell which process received its message ﬁrst.
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s09] But De is 0-valent, which implies Dee′ is also 0-valent, which contradicts De′e being 1-valent.
- CS-DIST-C01-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The FLP result extends to any asynchronous model in which it is impossible to tell which of two events happened first.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s20] The FLP results extends to any asynchronous model where it is impossible to tell which of two events happened ﬁrst.
- CS-DIST-C01-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The impossibility of agreement with one crash failure holds for the basic asynchronous model, and it can be circumvented by augmenting the model, for example with randomization or failure detectors.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0120-s12] 1Unless you augment the basic model in some way, say by adding randomization (Chapter 24) or failure detectors (Chapter 13).
- CS-DIST-C01-S3-03.r1a | S2
  ATOM: In asynchronous shared memory, two operations on different memory locations commute, as do two reads of the same location.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s22] For example, in asynchronous shared memory, if e and e′ are operations on diﬀerent memory locations, they commute (just like steps of diﬀerent processes), and if they are operations on the same location, either they commute (two reads) or only one process can tell whether both happened (with a write and a read, only the reader knows, and with two writes, only the ﬁrst writer knows).
- CS-DIST-C01-S3-03.r1b | S2
  ATOM: In asynchronous shared memory, for two operations on the same location that are a write and a read, only the reader can tell whether both operations happened; for two writes to the same location, only the first writer can tell whether both happened.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0124-s22] For example, in asynchronous shared memory, if e and e′ are operations on diﬀerent memory locations, they commute (just like steps of diﬀerent processes), and if they are operations on the same location, either they commute (two reads) or only one process can tell whether both happened (with a write and a read, only the reader knows, and with two writes, only the ﬁrst writer knows).
